CipherFlow

How this works

Source on GitHub · Report an issue

Build a graph

Every node is a step. Circles on a node are ports: inputs on the left, outputs on the right. Drag from an output to an input to draw a wire, and data flows along it. Add nodes from the list on the left — click one, drag it onto the canvas, or search for it. The list is grouped into Functions (blocks you build), Graph (the wiring nodes: Text Input / Output, File Input / Output, Join, Diff, Fstring, Math, Switch, Gate and Magic), Bundles (Compact, Expand, Pick and Fork, the nodes that carry lists) and Operations by category. The operations recreated from dCode and CacheSleuth come after the built-in ones in categories of their own, and the Symbols tab down the left edge of the canvas holds the symbol alphabets, which have a section below.

New here? Take the tour at the top of this panel walks through the canvas in seven steps — it also offers itself the first time the page is opened in a browser, and the ? button in the sidebar brings this panel back whenever you want it.

Text and file nodes are input and output

Text Input / Output and File Input / Output each have a port on both sides. With nothing piped into the left port, the text node shows a box for you to type your own value, and the file node shows a drop area. As soon as you pipe data in, that input wins and the node displays it instead — so either is the end of a chain on its own, with copy and save buttons on its preview. There is no separate Output node to add.

Preview controls

Every output box has Text and Raw views plus Hex, and a Full box that shows the whole result instead of cutting it off. When the result is an image, it renders in place and the tabs become Image, Raw and Hex. Raw shows the underlying bytes one character per byte; Hex writes the same bytes out in hexadecimal.

Operations and their arguments

Every operation carries a box for its own main input, and every argument it has gets a port of its own — a key, an IV, a password, but also a number, a switch or a dropdown. Type straight into a box and the node runs on what you typed, or wire another node's output into the port and the wire wins: the box dims and shows the value arriving on the wire, cut short if it runs long. A wired number is read as a number, a switch as on or off, and a wire into a dropdown picks whichever option it matches.

  • Join merges several wires into one in order, with an optional separator.
  • Diff puts two wires side by side: wire the value you expect into Expected and the value you got into Actual, and the node marks every character that differs, with a headline that reads identical or counts the changes. Bytes that are not text are compared as hex, so a changed byte shows up the same way. The marked reading flows out as text, so it can be copied or fed into the next step.
  • Fstring builds one string out of several: type a shape like Hello {input1}, key {input2} and each slot is filled from that numbered port — an f-string whose variables are wires.
  • Math uses the same numbered slots for arithmetic: type ({input1} * {input2}) - {input3} and it evaluates + - * / %, parentheses and ^ (or **) over the wired numbers.
  • Switch is a lookup table: wire a value into it, add a case per key with the value to hand on, and give an otherwise value for when nothing matches. Both halves of a case and the otherwise value take wires too — the wire wins while it is connected. With no otherwise at all (nothing wired and nothing typed) the input is passed straight through. Keys match exactly, once surrounding spaces are trimmed.
  • Gate hands nothing on until it is pressed, and a wire that loops back through a gate is not a cycle: each press lets the loop run one step further.

Lists on one wire

A bundle is a list carried on one wire, drawn thicker than a normal wire. The three bundle nodes sit together in the Bundles section at the top of the node list. Compact gathers everything plugged into it into a single bundle; its Inputs field sets how many ports it offers (1–32), and a port with no wire takes a string typed under it, so a literal can travel in the same bundle as wired values. Nested bundles are flattened, changing the count grows or shrinks the card to fit, and the preview numbers what the wire is carrying. Every port label on Compact and Expand is a text field: type over it to name that input or output, and the name is saved with the graph. Wires follow the port's position, not its name.

Expand spreads that bundle back over as many outputs as its own Outputs field says. Values past the number of outputs are dropped, and outputs with no value to carry come out empty. Lowering either count removes the wires on the ports that disappear.

Fork splits a text on a character — piped in, or typed on the node — and puts the parts on one bundled wire, so a comma-separated line becomes a list without being wired up part by part. Leave the box empty to split nothing.

Pick takes one value out of a bundle. Set Index to 1 for the first value; an index past the end gives an empty value. Its output is a single value, so the wire after it is a normal one.

An operation downstream of a bundle runs once per value and hands back a bundle, so a whole chain can work through a list without being wired once per item. That applies to arguments too: a bundle on a key, number or switch port runs the operation once per entry, two bundles are zipped by index, and a single value is broadcast against the whole list. A blank entry stays blank rather than failing the run.

Symbol alphabets

Down the left edge of the canvas is the Symbols tab, and behind it every symbol cipher this page can draw: 353 alphabets and 11,915 glyphs, from pigpen and the dancing men to Ogham, the Voynich hand, Dothraki, Teyvat, Wingdings, and the alphabets dCode and CacheSleuth publish art for. Search by name, or narrow the list with the tag pills — Thin or Bold, Straight or Curved, Dots, Pixels, Filled, Monochrome or Coloured. The pills in a group are alternatives, so choosing one releases the other; the count in the header, and a Reset beside it, say how much of the catalogue is left. With tags chosen every row carries how well it matches as a percentage, best first, and each row previews ten of its glyphs.

Click a row to drop that alphabet on the canvas as a node. The node is a transcription surface: click tiles in the grid and their letters are appended to the box under it, in the order you clicked them — type in the box instead if you already have the reading, and Clear empties it. The strip between grid and box repeats what you clicked as smaller labelled glyphs, and the text in the box is what leaves the node. A tile whose key is more than one character is separated from the one before it, so the reading cannot fuse.

Where both sources publish art for the same alphabet, a Source switch redraws the node with CacheSleuth's drawings or with dCode's. Where dCode also publishes a solved mapping for a cipher, a Variant switch on a dCode node captions each tile with that cryptogram's own letters instead of dCode's look-alike.

Magic

Magic lives in the Graph section of the node list (the wand icon). It is not one step in a chain: wire data into it and it runs every operation in the library over that input — including every Caesar shift from 1 to 25 — scores each result for how much it reads like real output, and ranks them. Set Show top to choose how many rows the node lists: it returns exactly that many, with findings first and less likely results filling the tail. Operations that land on the same text share one row, and decoders outrank encoders. Click a row to make that result the node's output and send it downstream.

Steganalysis, all local

The six audits below head the Multimedia category of the node list, above the operations they read bytes for.

  • PNG Chunks reads a PNG's container the way pngcheck does: every chunk with its length and CRC, the IHDR dimensions and colour type, tEXt/zTXt/iTXt text, and anything appended after IEND.
  • PDF Scan is the pdfid/pdfinfo view: header and version, object, stream and page counts, title/author strings, the risky markers (/JS, /OpenAction, /Launch, /EmbeddedFile, /Encrypt…), every %%EOF, and data appended after the last one.
  • Image Info is identify: format, dimensions, bit depth, frames and metadata for PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP and BMP.
  • Spectrogram draws audio as a frequency plot over time: scroll or pinch to zoom the time axis, hold Shift while scrolling to zoom the frequency band, drag the picture to move it and double-click to fit the file again. Its Merge channels switch folds left and right into one plot instead of giving each a lane, and the whole file leaves on the node's output wire as a PNG of the same plot.
  • Audio Levels is the loudness measurement — peak, RMS, DC offset, clipping and silence.

Each takes bytes on its left port and hands back one text report.

The rest of a sweep is already in the operation list, and these reports pipe into it: Strings for printable runs, Extract LSB and View Bit Plane for hidden bit layers, Extract RGBA and Randomize Colour Palette for channel and palette tricks, Extract EXIF for camera metadata, Scan for Embedded Files for signatures at any offset, and Extract Files for carving. Native tools such as steghide, outguess, zsteg and binwalk are separate programs with no browser equivalent, so they are not bundled — everything above runs in the page, with nothing uploaded.

Canvas, wires and view
  • Drag a node by its title bar to move it; drag the dotted canvas to pan, or scroll to zoom. Fit, in the bottom-left controls, frames the whole graph.
  • Drop an operation from the list onto a wire and it splices in where it landed: the wire splits and both halves reattach to the new node, so a step can be added to the middle of a chain without cutting the wire by hand. It is one undo step, and a node with no main input and output (a Note, a flow-control step, a two-sided tool) is refused and lands beside the wire instead.
  • The chevron in a node's header collapses it. Wires stay connected while collapsed.
  • A Note, from the Graph list, is a sticky note on the canvas: no ports and nothing to run, just somewhere to explain the graph. Click one of the six dots along its bottom edge to tint it; the words and the tint are saved with the graph, and a resized note gives the extra room to its text. Dragging the note card onto a node and dropping it there sticks the note under that node: the card under the pointer is outlined, and letting go turns the note into a caption hanging off that node's bottom edge. The node takes the note's tint, and the caption travels with it through drags, resizes, Snap and Order, is edited right there, and saves as part of the graph. Letting go anywhere else just moves the note. A node wears one caption; the × on it lets the note go and puts it back on the canvas as a card.
  • The eye beside it bypasses the node: its input passes through untouched, so one step can be switched off without unwiring it. The title is struck through while it is bypassed, and clicking the eye again runs it normally. A bypassed node is saved that way, and undo puts it back.
  • The snowflake beside the eye freezes the node: it holds the output it has at that moment and stops running, so an edit upstream cannot overwrite a reference value. The card wears an icy ring while it is frozen and the snowflake stays pressed in; click it again to let the node run. A freeze lasts for this session only — it is not written into the save, so a reload runs the node afresh.
  • Drag the bottom-right corner of a node to resize it. A long output scrolls inside the node instead of forcing it open, so it can be shrunk right down to a readable minimum. Double-click a title to rename any node, an operation or a function instance included.
  • Snap, beside Fit in the bottom-left controls, is a toggle. Turning it on puts every node on the graph back on the nearest grid dot and then keeps them there: dragged nodes track the grid as they move. It lights up while it is holding and the setting is remembered, so a reload comes back snapped. The same controls are the function editor's controls: Fit, Snap and zoom act on whichever graph is open.
  • Click a wire to select it — an × appears in the middle. Click the × to remove it, or double-click the wire.
  • The sun or moon icon in the sidebar switches between dark and light, and the choice is remembered.
  • On a phone the node list and the symbol alphabets are drawers: the two icons at either end of the toolbar open them, and placing a node closes the drawer again so the canvas comes back.

Several nodes at once
  • Shift+click a node to add it to the selection, or click it again to take it back out.
  • Shift+drag on the empty canvas draws a box and selects everything it touches.
  • Dragging any selected node moves the whole selection, and Delete removes all of it with its wires.
  • Ctrl+C, Ctrl+X and Ctrl+V copy, cut and paste the selection. The same JSON goes to your system clipboard, so a fragment can be pasted into another tab or a file and pasted back in.

Functions

A function is a graph of your own: build a body once, then place it like any other node. Press New function at the top of the node list to create one and its editor opens. Inside, the Function input node declares what the function takes — rename each row, give it a sample value, and add as many rows as you need — up to 32 inputs and 32 outputs on one function. Wire those into your body, and wire the body into the Function output node, which declares what it hands back. Run test tries the body on its sample values.

The editor window is the same canvas pointed at the definition, with its own node list down the right side — the same operations, search and gestures as the sidebar. The Nodes button in the header tucks the list away when you want the whole width for the canvas.

Press Done and the function appears in the node list: click or drag it onto the canvas to place an instance, which has one input port per declared input and one output port per declared output. Editing the definition updates every instance — the pencil in an instance's head (or the one beside the function in the node list) reopens the editor. A function cannot call itself, and definitions are saved inside the graph file, so a shared file keeps its functions.

Wiring a bundle into an instance runs the function once per entry and hands each declared output back as a bundle of the results. Two bundles wired into two inputs are zipped: run one takes entry 1 of both, run two takes entry 2 of both, and so on — so a function that needs a name and a key can be applied to two lists in step. When the lists differ in length the longer one decides, and an input whose list has run out gets an empty value.

Each declared input carries a test sample, which is what the body runs on when you press Run test. A sample can be Text you type, a File you attach, or a value piped in from a node in the body — wire something into the port on the sample row and it takes over. That is how a fixture is derived: build the value with nodes, pipe it in, and every instance can fall back to it. A function that works on an image, an archive or any other bytes can be tested on the real thing from inside the editor.

Tick Can be typed in on a declared input and every instance of the function grows a box for it, so a constant can be typed straight onto the node instead of needing something wired into the port. The box shows the input's test sample as its default, so you can see the value an untouched instance will run on; typing in the box overrides it, emptying the box puts the default back, and a wire into the port overrides both.

Running and shortcuts

With Auto-run on, the graph re-runs as you edit; Run forces a fresh pass. On a Mac, ⌘ works wherever Ctrl is listed.

  • Ctrl+K opens the command palette: run, fit, save, share, or jump to any operation, node, function or symbol cipher. Add Shift with one node selected and the same box replaces that node instead of adding another: the node keeps its place on the canvas, its input and output wires stay connected where the replacement has the same ports, and Enter on a command row still just runs the command. With one node selected it also offers that node's inverse: type “inverse” and pick Insert inverse to put the operation that undoes that step right after it — From Base64 after a To Base64, Leet Decode after Leet Encode, AES Decrypt after AES Encrypt — wired to its output and carrying the settings both steps share, or open the box with Shift and the same row swaps the node for its inverse in place. The partner is found by name, so every operation with an opposite in the library has one: To/From, Encode/Decode, Encrypt/Decrypt, Compress/Decompress, Escape/Unescape, Serialize/Deserialize, or a conversion that reads back the other way, like JSON to CSV after CSV to JSON. A step with no inverse — a hash, a parser — says so instead of guessing. With one wire selected instead, a node-shaped pick goes into that wire: it splits and the new step sits at the middle of the curve, the same splice as dropping it there. A node with no main input and output cannot go into a wire, so it is added where the pointer is and says why.
  • Ctrl+Alt+I adds the inverse of the selected node without opening the palette: one node selected, and the operation that undoes it is put right after it, wired to its output and carrying the settings both steps share. Add Shift and the node is swapped for its inverse in place instead. A step with no inverse says so instead of guessing.
  • Ctrl+Enter runs the graph
  • Ctrl+S saves in this browser
  • Ctrl+Shift+S downloads the graph
  • Ctrl+Z undoes; add Shift to redo
  • Ctrl+C, Ctrl+X and Ctrl+V copy, cut and paste
  • Delete or Backspace removes the selection or a wire
  • Escape closes a panel, cancels a wire, clears the selection
  • Shift+click or drag adds to the selection

Graphs and files

The File menu in the toolbar keeps your graphs. Load lists everything saved in this browser, newest first — click one to open it, or use the trash to delete it. New blank graph and Browse examples… replace whatever is on the canvas; the saved graphs stay.

Browse examples… opens the gallery: ready-made graphs for a ROT13 round trip, Base64 and Morse chains, a JWT, a symbol alphabet, an Fstring, a hex decode and the AES example. Each one opens as an ordinary graph with its wires in place, so it can be taken apart, renamed and saved like anything else.

Save keeps the graph under its name: Save “name” overwrites it and Save as… saves it under another name. A graph with no name asks for one, and the name it is saved under shows at the top of the menu. Separately, the canvas is autosaved as you work, so a reload brings back exactly what you had even if you never named it.

Import opens a .json graph file and Export downloads the current graph, or every saved graph in one file. Everything runs in this page — no data leaves it.

Copy as CyberChef recipe and Paste a CyberChef recipe…, in the File menu, move a straight chain of operations between CipherFlow and CyberChef. The copy writes the same JSON CyberChef's own Copy recipe button does — operation names, typed arguments, and a bypassed step as a disabled one — and the paste builds that chain left to right with its arguments filled in. Only one unbranched chain travels: a wire into an argument, a branch, a bundle or a CipherFlow-only operation is refused with a message rather than quietly dropped.

Copy share link puts the graph in the address bar as a link, compressed and encoded after the # — the part a browser never sends to the server. Opening one asks before it replaces the canvas; attached file bytes are not included, because a link is too small to carry them.

Checking the operations

The flask icon in the sidebar opens the verification lab: known-answer vectors, encode/decode round-trips and graph-wiring checks for every operation. Run all checks sweeps the lot; search or filter first and Run visible covers just those rows, while Retry failures re-runs what came back red. Results are kept in this browser, so closing the tab does not lose a long run, and the flask carries a count of unresolved failures. The filter beside the search narrows the rows to the Known-answer vectors, the Live probes or the Recreated ops — the dCode and CacheSleuth alphabets — so the recreated work is never mixed in with the built-in checks.
